subject: grade-11-physical-sciences
description: Grade 11 Physical Sciences skill tree (CAPS FET). 15 levels (one per CAPS topic) split across Physics (P1) and Chemistry (P2), covering the six CAPS knowledge areas: Mechanics, Waves/Sound/Light, Electricity & Magnetism, Matter & Materials, Chemical Change, Chemical Systems. 24 atomic skills. Tap-native bank (choice / numeric / sequence — no free-text). Items live in data/grade-11-physical-sciences-question-banks/<skill-id>.json.

levels.title: Vectors in Two Dimensions
levels.description: Resultant of perpendicular vectors (graphically and by Pythagoras/trigonometry) and resolving a vector into perpendicular components.

atomic_skills.title: Find the resultant of perpendicular vectors and resolve a vector into components
atomic_skills.description: Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant of two perpendicular vectors using Pythagoras and trigonometry; resolve a single vector into its perpendicular (x and y) components.

error_signatures.description: Adds perpendicular vector magnitudes directly instead of using Pythagoras
error_signatures.example: Says a 3 N and 4 N perpendicular pair give a 7 N resultant

error_signatures.description: Swaps sin and cos when resolving components
error_signatures.example: Uses Fcosθ for the vertical component measured from the horizontal

error_signatures.description: Omits the direction (angle) of the resultant
error_signatures.example: Gives the resultant as 5 N with no angle

error_signatures.description: Resolves into components that do not add back to the original vector
error_signatures.example: Chooses components larger than the original vector

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: For perpendicular vectors: resultant magnitude R = √(Ax² + Ay²); direction from tanθ = opposite/adjacent. To resolve: component along the angle = Fcosθ, perpendicular component = Fsinθ (θ measured from that axis). Components are always SMALLER than the original vector and must add back to it.

levels.title: Newton's Laws and Application of Newton's Laws
levels.description: Newton's three laws, free-body diagrams, friction (static and kinetic), single bodies, connected bodies and inclined planes, and Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation.

atomic_skills.title: State Newton's laws, draw free-body diagrams and apply Fnet = ma to a single body
atomic_skills.description: State Newton's First, Second and Third Laws in CAPS wording and identify which applies; draw a free-body diagram showing all forces on one object; apply Fnet = ma to a single body on a horizontal or vertical surface (including weight, normal force, applied force and friction).

error_signatures.description: Treats a Newton's Third Law pair as acting on the same body
error_signatures.example: Says the normal force and weight on a book are an action-reaction pair

error_signatures.description: Uses weight instead of net force in Fnet = ma
error_signatures.example: Sets mg = ma for a block being pushed across a floor

error_signatures.description: Includes a force the body exerts on something else in its FBD
error_signatures.example: Adds 'force of block on table' to the block's free-body diagram

error_signatures.description: Treats friction as acting in the direction of motion
error_signatures.example: Adds friction to the applied force

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: 1st law = no net force ⇒ velocity unchanged; 2nd law = Fnet = ma; 3rd law = equal, opposite forces on DIFFERENT bodies. On a free-body diagram draw only the forces acting ON the chosen object, from a single point. Sum forces along the direction of motion with consistent signs; friction always opposes motion.

atomic_skills.title: Apply Newton's laws to connected bodies, inclined planes and friction
atomic_skills.description: Solve Fnet = ma problems for objects connected by strings/pulleys (shared acceleration, single tension) and for bodies on inclined planes; resolve weight into mg sinθ and mg cosθ; apply static and kinetic friction (f = μN).

error_signatures.description: Uses mg as the down-slope force instead of mg sinθ
error_signatures.example: Sets the force along the incline equal to mg

error_signatures.description: Swaps sin and cos for the incline components
error_signatures.example: Writes parallel component = mg cosθ

error_signatures.description: Solves one connected body in isolation without the system acceleration
error_signatures.example: Uses only one block's forces to find the shared acceleration

error_signatures.description: Confuses static and kinetic friction or uses the wrong coefficient
error_signatures.example: Uses μ_k while the object is still stationary

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Connected bodies: treat the whole system as one mass to get acceleration, then isolate one body for the tension (same string ⇒ same tension). On an incline tilt your axes with the slope: down-slope weight component = mg sinθ, perpendicular = mg cosθ. Friction f = μN; static friction (μ_s) up to the point of slipping, kinetic (μ_k) once moving.

atomic_skills.title: Apply Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
atomic_skills.description: Use F = GMm/r² to find the gravitational force between two masses and analyse how it changes with mass or separation; relate weight to gravitational force and calculate g = GM/r²; distinguish mass and weight.

error_signatures.description: Forgets to square r in F = GMm/r²
error_signatures.example: Writes F = GMm/r

error_signatures.description: Doubles r and predicts the force halves
error_signatures.example: Predicts F → F/2 when separation doubles instead of F/4

error_signatures.description: Says mass changes from planet to planet
error_signatures.example: States an astronaut's mass is less on the Moon

error_signatures.description: Uses diameter instead of radius (distance from centre) for r
error_signatures.example: Substitutes a planet's diameter into g = GM/r²

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: F = GMm/r² is an inverse-square law: r doubles ⇒ F divides by 4; r halves ⇒ F ×4. Mass stays the same everywhere; WEIGHT (w = mg) changes with g. g = GM/r² where r is measured from the CENTRE of the planet.

levels.title: Geometrical Optics
levels.description: Refraction of light, refractive index, Snell's Law, the critical angle and total internal reflection.

atomic_skills.title: Apply refraction and Snell's Law
atomic_skills.description: Describe refraction in terms of change of speed at a boundary; define refractive index (n = c/v); apply Snell's Law n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂ to find an unknown angle or refractive index; predict whether light bends towards or away from the normal.

error_signatures.description: Measures the angle of incidence from the surface instead of the normal
error_signatures.example: Uses the angle between the ray and the boundary in Snell's Law

error_signatures.description: Says light bends away from the normal when entering a denser medium
error_signatures.example: Predicts light bends away from the normal going from air into glass

error_signatures.description: Inverts the refractive index n = c/v
error_signatures.example: Calculates n as v/c

error_signatures.description: Mixes up which medium is n₁ and n₂
error_signatures.example: Swaps the two media in n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Angles are always measured from the NORMAL (perpendicular to the surface). Refractive index n = c/v ≥ 1 (denser medium = larger n, slower light). Entering a DENSER medium ⇒ light bends TOWARDS the normal; into a less dense medium ⇒ AWAY. Apply n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂ with subscript 1 for the incident side.

atomic_skills.title: Apply the critical angle and total internal reflection
atomic_skills.description: Define the critical angle and total internal reflection; calculate the critical angle using sinθc = n₂/n₁; state the two conditions for total internal reflection and apply it to optical fibres.

error_signatures.description: Says total internal reflection happens going from a less dense to a denser medium
error_signatures.example: Predicts TIR when light passes from air into glass

error_signatures.description: States only one of the two conditions for TIR
error_signatures.example: Says TIR needs only that the angle exceeds the critical angle

error_signatures.description: Inverts the critical-angle ratio
error_signatures.example: Uses sinθc = n₁/n₂ instead of n₂/n₁

error_signatures.description: Says light refracts out when the angle exceeds the critical angle
error_signatures.example: Predicts the ray still emerges at angles above θc

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Total internal reflection needs BOTH: light travelling from a denser to a less dense medium AND the angle of incidence greater than the critical angle. Critical angle: sinθc = n₂/n₁ (n₂ = less dense medium). Above θc, no light escapes — it all reflects internally (used in optical fibres).

levels.title: 2D and 3D Wavefronts
levels.description: Wavefronts, Huygens' principle and diffraction of waves through a single slit (qualitative).

atomic_skills.title: Describe wavefronts, Huygens' principle and diffraction
atomic_skills.description: Define a wavefront; apply Huygens' principle (each point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets); describe diffraction through a single slit and predict qualitatively how slit width and wavelength affect the amount of diffraction.

error_signatures.description: Says a wider slit produces more diffraction
error_signatures.example: Predicts more spreading when the gap is made larger

error_signatures.description: Says diffraction changes the wavelength of the wave
error_signatures.example: Claims the wave's wavelength increases after passing the slit

error_signatures.description: Says diffraction only happens with light, not sound or water
error_signatures.example: States only light waves diffract

error_signatures.description: Reverses the effect of wavelength on diffraction
error_signatures.example: Says shorter wavelength diffracts more for the same slit

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: A wavefront joins points in phase; Huygens: every point on it acts as a source of new wavelets. Diffraction = waves spreading as they pass an edge/slit. MORE diffraction when the slit is NARROW or the wavelength is LONG (when slit width ≈ wavelength). The wavelength itself is unchanged. All waves diffract (water, sound, light).

levels.title: Electrostatics
levels.description: Coulomb's Law (force between point charges) and the electric field of point charges.

atomic_skills.title: Apply Coulomb's Law to the force between point charges
atomic_skills.description: Use F = kQ₁Q₂/r² to calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between two point charges and decide whether it is attractive or repulsive; analyse how the force changes when charge or separation changes.

error_signatures.description: Forgets to square r in Coulomb's Law
error_signatures.example: Writes F = kQ₁Q₂/r

error_signatures.description: Treats a negative product of charges as a force direction
error_signatures.example: Reports F = -2 N and calls that the direction

error_signatures.description: Doubles a charge and predicts the force doubles only if separation also changes
error_signatures.example: Cannot predict F when Q₁ doubles and r halves

error_signatures.description: Leaves charges in microcoulombs without converting
error_signatures.example: Uses 5 instead of 5×10⁻⁶ C

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: F = kQ₁Q₂/r² gives a MAGNITUDE (use absolute charge values); sign of charges only tells you attractive (opposite) or repulsive (same). Don't forget r². Convert µC to C (×10⁻⁶). Inverse-square in r and proportional to each charge: e.g. Q₁ doubles ⇒ F doubles; r halves ⇒ F ×4.

atomic_skills.title: Calculate and describe the electric field of point charges
atomic_skills.description: Define electric field; use E = kQ/r² for a single point charge and E = F/q; draw electric field patterns; combine fields from charges on a line to find the net field at a point.

error_signatures.description: Adds field magnitudes when the fields point in opposite directions
error_signatures.example: Reports net E as the sum when the two fields oppose

error_signatures.description: Draws field lines pointing into a positive charge
error_signatures.example: Shows arrows towards a positive charge

error_signatures.description: Uses E = kQ/r² with the test charge instead of the source charge
error_signatures.example: Substitutes the test charge q for Q

error_signatures.description: Treats electric field as a scalar
error_signatures.example: Ignores direction when combining two fields

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Electric field is a VECTOR. From a + charge, field points OUTWARD; from a − charge, INWARD. For a single charge E = kQ/r² (Q = source charge); the force on a test charge is F = qE. Combine fields as vectors: same direction ⇒ add; opposite ⇒ subtract.

levels.title: Electromagnetism
levels.description: The magnetic field associated with a current-carrying conductor and solenoid; Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction (qualitative).

atomic_skills.title: Describe the magnetic field of a current-carrying conductor and solenoid
atomic_skills.description: Describe and predict the magnetic field pattern around a straight current-carrying conductor and inside/around a solenoid; apply the right-hand rule to find field direction; describe factors affecting the strength of an electromagnet.

error_signatures.description: Says a steady current produces no magnetic field
error_signatures.example: Claims only moving magnets, not currents, make fields

error_signatures.description: Applies the right-hand rule with the wrong current direction (conventional vs electron flow)
error_signatures.example: Uses electron flow direction in the right-hand rule

error_signatures.description: Draws the field around a straight wire as straight lines instead of concentric circles
error_signatures.example: Shows the field as parallel lines along the wire

error_signatures.description: Says reversing the current leaves the field direction unchanged
error_signatures.example: Predicts the same field direction after reversing the current

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: A current ALWAYS produces a magnetic field. Around a straight wire the field is CONCENTRIC CIRCLES; use the right-hand rule (thumb = conventional current, fingers curl = field). A solenoid behaves like a bar magnet. Reversing the current reverses the field. Stronger field: more current, more turns, or an iron core.

atomic_skills.title: Apply Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction (qualitative)
atomic_skills.description: State Faraday's Law (a changing magnetic flux induces an EMF) and apply it qualitatively; relate induced EMF to the rate of change of flux, number of turns and field strength; describe how moving a magnet relative to a coil induces a current.

error_signatures.description: Says a stationary magnet inside a coil induces a current
error_signatures.example: Predicts a current when the magnet is held still in the coil

error_signatures.description: Says induced EMF depends on the flux itself, not its rate of change
error_signatures.example: States a large steady flux gives a large EMF

error_signatures.description: Says faster movement of the magnet gives a smaller induced EMF
error_signatures.example: Predicts less EMF when the magnet moves quickly

error_signatures.description: Ignores the number of turns when comparing two coils
error_signatures.example: Says two coils with different turns give the same EMF

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Induction needs a CHANGING magnetic flux through the coil — a stationary magnet induces nothing. Induced EMF is larger when the flux changes FASTER, the field is stronger, or there are MORE turns. Move a magnet in/out of a coil ⇒ changing flux ⇒ induced EMF and current.

levels.title: Electric Circuits
levels.description: Ohm's Law (ohmic vs non-ohmic conductors), resistance in series and parallel, and electrical power and energy.

atomic_skills.title: Apply Ohm's Law and resistance in series and parallel circuits
atomic_skills.description: State Ohm's Law and distinguish ohmic from non-ohmic conductors; apply V = IR; calculate total resistance for series (R = R₁ + R₂ + …) and parallel (1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …) combinations and reduce mixed networks.

error_signatures.description: Adds parallel resistances directly
error_signatures.example: Reports two 4 Ω resistors in parallel as 8 Ω

error_signatures.description: Forgets to invert 1/R after summing reciprocals
error_signatures.example: Reports 1/R = 0.5 as R = 0.5 Ω

error_signatures.description: Says a non-ohmic conductor obeys V = IR at all currents
error_signatures.example: Treats a light bulb filament as ohmic across all voltages

error_signatures.description: Rearranges V = IR incorrectly
error_signatures.example: Writes I = V × R

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Ohm's Law: V = IR, valid for OHMIC conductors at constant temperature (straight V-I graph through the origin). Non-ohmic (e.g. bulb) curves. SERIES: resistances ADD. PARALLEL: add reciprocals then INVERT (1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂…). Reduce mixed circuits one block at a time.

atomic_skills.title: Calculate electrical power and energy
atomic_skills.description: Use P = VI, P = I²R, P = V²/R to calculate power, and W = Pt = VIt for energy; relate to the cost of electricity (kWh).

error_signatures.description: Chooses a power formula using a quantity not given
error_signatures.example: Uses P = V²/R when only current and resistance are known

error_signatures.description: Forgets to square the current or voltage
error_signatures.example: Writes P = IR instead of P = I²R

error_signatures.description: Mixes time units in W = Pt
error_signatures.example: Uses minutes with watts and seconds inconsistently

error_signatures.description: Confuses power and energy
error_signatures.example: Reports an answer in watts when energy in joules is required

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Pick the power formula matching your known quantities: P = VI, P = I²R, or P = V²/R. Energy W = Pt = VIt (use seconds for joules). Power is the RATE of using energy (W); energy is power × time (J or kWh). 1 kWh = energy of 1 kW running for 1 hour.

levels.title: Atomic Combinations (Molecular Structure)
levels.description: Chemical bonding revisited — Lewis diagrams and bond formation; molecular shape (VSEPR), electronegativity and bond polarity.

atomic_skills.title: Draw Lewis diagrams and describe covalent bond formation
atomic_skills.description: Draw Lewis (electron) diagrams for molecules and polyatomic ions; identify bonding and lone pairs; describe single, double, triple and dative (coordinate) covalent bonds; relate bond energy and bond length.

error_signatures.description: Gives an atom the wrong number of bonds (breaks the octet)
error_signatures.example: Draws nitrogen with four single bonds and no lone pair in NH₃

error_signatures.description: Confuses bonding pairs and lone pairs
error_signatures.example: Counts a lone pair as a bond

error_signatures.description: Says a shorter bond is weaker
error_signatures.example: Claims a triple bond is weaker than a single bond

error_signatures.description: Cannot identify a dative (coordinate) bond
error_signatures.example: Treats the extra bond in NH₄⁺ as identical-origin to the others

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Each atom aims for a full outer shell (octet; H = 2). Count valence electrons, form shared pairs (single/double/triple), and place remaining electrons as lone pairs. A dative/coordinate bond = both shared electrons come from ONE atom (e.g. NH₄⁺). More bonds between two atoms ⇒ SHORTER and STRONGER bond.

atomic_skills.title: Predict molecular shape (VSEPR) and bond polarity
atomic_skills.description: Use VSEPR theory to predict the shape of a molecule from its bonding and lone pairs; use electronegativity differences to classify bonds as non-polar, polar covalent or ionic; determine whether a molecule is polar overall.

error_signatures.description: Ignores lone pairs when predicting shape
error_signatures.example: Calls water linear because it has two bonds

error_signatures.description: Says a molecule with polar bonds is always polar
error_signatures.example: Calls CO₂ a polar molecule

error_signatures.description: Uses the wrong electronegativity-difference cut-offs
error_signatures.example: Calls a 0.2 difference bond ionic

error_signatures.description: Confuses molecular shapes (e.g. tetrahedral vs trigonal pyramidal)
error_signatures.example: Calls NH₃ tetrahedral because nitrogen has four electron pairs

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: VSEPR: electron pairs (bonding AND lone) repel and spread out. Count pairs around the central atom: 2 = linear, 3 = trigonal planar, 4 = tetrahedral; lone pairs change the SHAPE name (e.g. 4 pairs with 1 lone = trigonal pyramidal like NH₃; 2 lone = bent like H₂O). Bigger electronegativity difference ⇒ more polar (large difference ⇒ ionic). A molecule is non-polar overall if its polar bonds are SYMMETRICAL and cancel (e.g. CO₂).

levels.title: Intermolecular Forces
levels.description: Intermolecular and interatomic forces; relating intermolecular forces to the physical properties of substances (melting/boiling points, vapour pressure, solubility).

atomic_skills.title: Identify intermolecular forces and relate them to physical properties
atomic_skills.description: Identify the intermolecular forces (London/dispersion, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding, ion-dipole) present in a substance from its structure; relate the strength of these forces to melting and boiling points, vapour pressure, solubility and other physical properties.

error_signatures.description: Says all polar molecules show hydrogen bonding
error_signatures.example: Claims HCl has hydrogen bonds

error_signatures.description: Confuses intermolecular forces with covalent bonds
error_signatures.example: Says boiling water breaks the O–H bonds

error_signatures.description: Says stronger forces give a higher vapour pressure
error_signatures.example: Predicts water has a higher vapour pressure than ether

error_signatures.description: Says non-polar molecules have no intermolecular forces
error_signatures.example: States that methane molecules have no forces between them

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: London (dispersion) forces are in ALL molecules (stronger in bigger molecules). Dipole-dipole adds in polar molecules. Hydrogen bonding only when H is bonded to N, O or F — the strongest of the three. Boiling/melting a substance breaks the INTERMOLECULAR forces, not the covalent bonds. Stronger forces ⇒ higher boiling/melting point, LOWER vapour pressure.

levels.title: Ideal Gases and Thermal Properties
levels.description: The gas laws (Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac), the general and ideal gas equations, and the kinetic theory of gases.

atomic_skills.title: Apply the gas laws (Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac) and the general gas equation
atomic_skills.description: Apply Boyle's Law (pV = constant), Charles' Law (V/T = constant) and Gay-Lussac's/pressure law (p/T = constant), and the combined general gas equation p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂, converting temperatures to kelvin.

error_signatures.description: Uses temperature in degrees Celsius instead of kelvin
error_signatures.example: Substitutes 25 instead of 298 K in Charles' Law

error_signatures.description: Says pressure and volume are directly proportional at constant temperature
error_signatures.example: Predicts volume increases when pressure increases (Boyle)

error_signatures.description: Mixes up which quantity is held constant
error_signatures.example: Uses Boyle's Law for a constant-pressure process

error_signatures.description: Sets up the combined equation with mismatched subscripts
error_signatures.example: Pairs p₁ with V₂ in p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: ALWAYS convert temperature to kelvin (K = °C + 273). Boyle (constant T): p and V are INVERSELY proportional (pV constant). Charles (constant p): V/T constant. Gay-Lussac (constant V): p/T constant. Combined: p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂ — keep each state's quantities together.

atomic_skills.title: Apply the ideal gas equation and kinetic theory of gases
atomic_skills.description: Use the ideal gas equation pV = nRT to find pressure, volume, temperature or amount; describe the kinetic theory of gases and the assumptions of an ideal gas, and explain deviations from ideal behaviour.

error_signatures.description: Mixes units (uses cm³ or kPa inconsistently with R)
error_signatures.example: Uses volume in dm³ with R for SI units without converting

error_signatures.description: Forgets to convert temperature to kelvin in pV = nRT
error_signatures.example: Uses Celsius for T

error_signatures.description: Says real gases behave most ideally at high pressure and low temperature
error_signatures.example: Claims ideal behaviour improves as a gas is compressed and cooled

error_signatures.description: States an incorrect assumption of the kinetic theory
error_signatures.example: Says ideal gas particles have significant volume and attractions

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: pV = nRT — match units to R (SI: Pa, m³, K) or convert. T must be in kelvin. Ideal gas assumptions: particles have negligible volume, no intermolecular forces, collisions are perfectly elastic, constant random motion. Real gases deviate most at HIGH pressure and LOW temperature (particles close together).

levels.title: Quantitative Aspects of Chemical Change (Stoichiometry)
levels.description: Molar volume of gases and concentration; limiting reagents, percentage yield, percentage purity, empirical and molecular formulae and water of crystallisation.

atomic_skills.title: Apply moles, molar volume and concentration in calculations
atomic_skills.description: Use n = m/M, molar volume of a gas (n = V/Vm), concentration c = n/V and number of particles to convert between quantities; combine with mole ratios from a balanced equation.

error_signatures.description: Inverts n = m/M or c = n/V
error_signatures.example: Calculates moles as M/m

error_signatures.description: Ignores the mole ratio from the balanced equation
error_signatures.example: Assumes 1:1 when the equation gives 2:1

error_signatures.description: Mixes volume units (cm³ vs dm³)
error_signatures.example: Uses 500 cm³ as 500 dm³

error_signatures.description: Applies molar volume at non-STP conditions
error_signatures.example: Uses 22.4 dm³/mol for a gas not at STP

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Core conversions: n = m/M; c = n/V (convert cm³→dm³ by ÷1000); for gases at STP, n = V/22.4. For reactions: convert known to moles → multiply by the MOLE RATIO from the balanced equation → convert to the quantity asked.

atomic_skills.title: Solve limiting reagent, percentage yield, percentage purity and empirical formula problems
atomic_skills.description: Identify the limiting reagent and use it to find product amounts; calculate percentage yield and percentage purity; determine empirical and molecular formulae and the formula of a hydrate (water of crystallisation).

error_signatures.description: Picks the reactant with the smaller mass as limiting without using moles and the ratio
error_signatures.example: Calls the lighter reactant limiting by mass alone

error_signatures.description: Calculates percentage yield as theoretical/actual
error_signatures.example: Inverts the yield fraction

error_signatures.description: Does not divide by the smallest mole value for empirical formula
error_signatures.example: Uses raw mole values as subscripts

error_signatures.description: Confuses percentage yield and percentage purity
error_signatures.example: Uses the purity formula to find yield

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Limiting reagent: convert BOTH reactants to moles, divide each by its coefficient — the smaller value is limiting and sets the product. % yield = (actual/theoretical) × 100. % purity = (pure mass/total sample mass) × 100. Empirical formula: moles of each element ÷ smallest, round to whole numbers. Hydrate: find the mole ratio of salt to water.

levels.title: Energy and Chemical Change
levels.description: Exothermic and endothermic reactions, activation energy, bond energy and potential-energy diagrams.

atomic_skills.title: Classify reactions as exothermic/endothermic and interpret potential-energy diagrams
atomic_skills.description: Classify reactions as exothermic or endothermic from ΔH or a potential-energy diagram; relate bond breaking (absorbs energy) and bond forming (releases energy) to the net energy change; identify activation energy, the activated complex, and the heat of reaction on a potential-energy graph.

error_signatures.description: Swaps the sign of ΔH for exothermic and endothermic
error_signatures.example: Says exothermic reactions have a positive ΔH

error_signatures.description: Says bond breaking releases energy
error_signatures.example: States energy is given out when bonds break

error_signatures.description: Reads activation energy as the heat of reaction on the graph
error_signatures.example: Calls the products-minus-reactants gap the activation energy

error_signatures.description: Says a catalyst changes ΔH
error_signatures.example: Predicts a more exothermic reaction when a catalyst is added

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Bond BREAKING absorbs energy; bond FORMING releases energy. Exothermic = releases energy, products LOWER than reactants, ΔH NEGATIVE. Endothermic = absorbs energy, products HIGHER, ΔH POSITIVE. On a potential-energy diagram: activation energy = reactants up to the peak (activated complex); heat of reaction (ΔH) = products minus reactants. A catalyst lowers activation energy only — ΔH is unchanged.

levels.title: Acids and Bases
levels.description: Acids and bases — their reactions (with metals, carbonates and bases) and the products of neutralisation reactions.

atomic_skills.title: Predict the products of acid reactions and neutralisation
atomic_skills.description: Identify common acids and bases; predict the products of acid + metal, acid + metal oxide, acid + metal hydroxide (neutralisation) and acid + metal carbonate/hydrogen carbonate reactions; write balanced equations for these reactions.

error_signatures.description: Forgets a product of an acid-carbonate reaction
error_signatures.example: Omits CO₂ and water from acid + carbonate

error_signatures.description: Says acid + metal produces water
error_signatures.example: Writes water as a product of acid + magnesium

error_signatures.description: Names the wrong salt for the acid used
error_signatures.example: Gives a chloride salt from sulphuric acid

error_signatures.description: Leaves the neutralisation equation unbalanced
error_signatures.example: Writes HCl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + H₂O unbalanced

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Acid + metal ⇒ salt + HYDROGEN gas. Acid + metal oxide / metal hydroxide ⇒ salt + WATER (neutralisation). Acid + carbonate (or hydrogen carbonate) ⇒ salt + water + CARBON DIOXIDE. The salt's anion comes from the acid: HCl→chloride, H₂SO₄→sulphate, HNO₃→nitrate. Then balance.

levels.title: Redox Reactions
levels.description: Oxidation numbers, identifying oxidation and reduction, oxidising and reducing agents, and distinguishing redox from non-redox reactions.

atomic_skills.title: Assign oxidation numbers and identify oxidation, reduction and agents
atomic_skills.description: Assign oxidation numbers using the rules; identify which species is oxidised and which is reduced; identify the oxidising agent and reducing agent; classify a reaction as redox or non-redox.

error_signatures.description: Assigns the wrong oxidation number to oxygen or hydrogen in a special case
error_signatures.example: Gives oxygen −2 in a peroxide

error_signatures.description: Swaps oxidation and reduction
error_signatures.example: Calls a decrease in oxidation number oxidation

error_signatures.description: Identifies the oxidising agent as the species oxidised
error_signatures.example: Calls the reducing agent the one that gets reduced

error_signatures.description: Oxidation numbers in an ion do not sum to its charge
error_signatures.example: Assigns numbers in SO₄²⁻ that add up to 0

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Rules: free element = 0; group 1 = +1, group 2 = +2; O = −2 (except peroxides −1); H = +1 (except metal hydrides −1); sum = 0 for a molecule or = the charge for an ion. OXIDATION = oxidation number INCREASES (loses electrons); REDUCTION = DECREASES (gains electrons). The OXIDISING agent is itself REDUCED; the REDUCING agent is itself OXIDISED. If no oxidation numbers change, it is non-redox.

levels.title: Exploiting the Lithosphere
levels.description: The lithosphere as a chemical system — the minerals and mining industry of South Africa, extraction of metals and the associated energy and environmental considerations.

atomic_skills.title: Describe mining, mineral extraction and its impact in the lithosphere
atomic_skills.description: Describe the lithosphere and South Africa's mineral wealth; outline how selected minerals/metals are mined and extracted; describe the energy requirements and environmental and social impacts of mining and the need for responsible exploitation.

error_signatures.description: Confuses the lithosphere with the hydrosphere or atmosphere
error_signatures.example: Says the lithosphere is all the water on Earth

error_signatures.description: Says a metal is found in the ground as the pure element
error_signatures.example: Claims iron is mined as pure iron metal

error_signatures.description: Says mining has no environmental impact
error_signatures.example: States mining does not affect water or air quality

error_signatures.description: Mismatches a mineral with how it is extracted
error_signatures.example: Says gold is extracted by simple heating in air

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: The lithosphere = the solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth, rich in minerals. Most metals occur as ORES (compounds), not pure elements, and must be extracted (e.g. by reduction or electrolysis), which needs ENERGY. Mining brings economic benefit but has environmental and social costs (water, air, land), so it must be done responsibly and sustainably.
